name: Horsetail (Equisetum)
short: Case reports: liver injury and severe low blood sodium (title-only letters), pancreatitis, and possible loss of HIV control with antiretroviral drugs. Trials of up to 3 months: few adverse events.
text: Serious harms come from single case reports, which cannot show cause: a 2012 letter titled 'Equisetum arvense (Field Horsetail)-induced liver injury' and a 2018 letter titled 'Severe Hyponatremia After Drinking Horsetail Juice' (both title-only records with no abstract); a 56-year-old woman with recurrent mild acute pancreatitis whose episodes stopped after she stopped regular horsetail infusions (teas); and a case report that raises, as a possible mechanism, vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency from the thiaminase enzyme in horsetail in a mother who took horsetail remedies before and during pregnancy along with alcohol, and whose daughter has autism spectrum disorder; the authors advise avoiding herbal supplements with suspected or potential toxicity during pregnancy. Interaction: a report of 2 people with HIV describes a possible interaction in which a horsetail-containing supplement may have led to virological breakthrough (HIV no longer controlled) on long-standing antiretroviral regimens including efavirenz, and the authors advise clinicians to avoid the combination when possible. In trials of a standardized dry extract of Equisetum arvense (the abstracts do not state the route), a 3-month randomized trial in 58 adults with stage 1 high blood pressure found adverse events in 3.58% with horsetail and 4.68% with hydrochlorothiazide (not significantly different) and no significant before-and-after differences in biochemical tests, signs of acute toxicity or kidney, liver and blood measures, and a 4-day crossover trial in 36 healthy men reported rare minor adverse events and no changes in clinical examinations or laboratory tests. In an 8-week placebo-controlled trial of a three-herb combination including horsetail stem (with Crataeva nurvala and Lindera aggregata) on symptoms of overactive bladder and urinary incontinence, in 150 participants (mean age 63.5 years), no significant side effects leading to withdrawal were observed.
